original_question: Does there exist an integer k such that if two positive integers m and n satisfy R(m + i) = R(n + i) for every i = 0, ..., k - 1, then m = n?
target_in_paper: Conjecture 2.2 (Erdős–Woods) in §2.1, not the broader arithmetic-progression generalization asked immediately afterward.
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the core logical structure of the paper’s statement: it asks for the existence of a fixed integer k, quantifies over positive integers m and n, compares the values of R on the k consecutive integers m, m+1, ..., m+k-1 and n, n+1, ..., n+k-1, and concludes that this should force m = n.
missing_details: The notation R(t) must be defined. In the paper, R(t) denotes the radical (square-free part) of the positive integer t: R(t) = product of all primes p dividing t.
The paper states that k should be a positive integer.
To make the quantifiers fully stand-alone, it should say explicitly: for all positive integers m and n.
The scope should remain exactly the consecutive-integers case (step size 1). The paper treats the arithmetic-progression version with parameters d and d' as a separate, broader question.
If desired for readability, one may spell out that R(a) = R(b) means that a and b have the same set of prime divisors; this is implicit from the definition of R.
refined_question: Let R(t) = ∏_{p|t} p denote the radical (square-free part) of a positive integer t. Does there exist a positive integer k such that, for all positive integers m and n, the conditions R(m+i) = R(n+i) for every i = 0, 1, ..., k-1 imply m = n?
justification: The draft is essentially a near-verbatim restatement of the paper’s Erdős–Woods conjecture. The only mathematically essential omission is the definition of R. The nearby context in §2.1 defines R as the radical, introduces the conjecture in exactly this consecutive-shift form, and then separately discusses both the abc-based evidence that k = 3 should work up to finitely many exceptions and Shorey’s distinct arithmetic-progression generalization, so the refined version should stay narrowly with the original consecutive-integers problem.

citations.label: discussion after Conjecture 2.2: abc implies k = 3 except possibly finitely many exceptions; k = 2 is not admissible
